name: Program Analysis
description: Static/dynamic analysis, symbolic execution, taint tracking, and bug detection for security.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers in this set, from USENIX Security 2018, show program analysis maturing into a practical, security-driven discipline. A central thread is making heavyweight techniques scale to real bugs. QSYM: A Practical Concolic Execution Engine Tailored for Hybrid Fuzzing (2018) is the anchor: it married concolic execution to fuzzing so the symbolic engine only solved the hard branches, turning a slow technique into a usable one. Alongside it, 2018 work pushed analysis into specific exploit domains: teEther (2018) automatically generated exploits for Ethereum smart contracts, NAVEX (2018) chained static and dynamic analysis to build exploits for dynamic web apps, and HeapHopper (2018) and Automatic Heap Layout Manipulation for Exploitation (2018) brought model checking and search to memory-allocator security. Meta-analysis appeared too, with Discovering Flaws in Security-Focused Static Analysis Tools for Android (2018) using systematic mutation to test the testers.

By 2019 the field broadened from "find any crash" toward semantic and domain-specific bugs and toward smarter fuzzing. Detecting Missing-Check Bugs (2019) and PeX (2019) inferred which security and permission checks a program ought to perform, catching logic flaws static tools had missed, while DEEPVSA (2019) and GRIMOIRE (2019) injected deep learning and structure synthesis into binary analysis and fuzzing respectively. A debloating sub-theme emerged as attack-surface reduction, with RAZOR (2019) and Less is More (2019) trimming unused code from binaries and web apps. This momentum carried into 2020, where data-flow-aware fuzzing matured in GREYONE (2020), firmware became analyzable via re-hosting in HALucinator (2020), fuzzer construction itself was automated by FuzzGen (2020), and analysis spread to privacy policies (PoliCheck, 2020), patch-based vulnerability signatures (MVP, 2020), and post-crash root-cause explanation (AURORA, 2020).

The most recent years show the area specializing and, increasingly, fusing learning with classical analysis. Smart-contract and blockchain security consolidated through TXSPECTOR (2020), SmarTest (2021), which guided symbolic execution with a language model, and EOSAFE (2021). Fuzzing kept refining its feedback signals, as in The Use of Likely Invariants as Feedback for Fuzzers (2021), while access-control reasoning scaled to cloud microservices in Automatic Policy Generation for Inter-Service Access Control (2021). By 2023-2024 the center of gravity tilts toward learned representations of code: VulChecker (2023) localizes vulnerabilities via graph neural networks, and Code is not Natural Language (2024) builds semantics-oriented graph representations for binary similarity detection. The arc runs from making symbolic and dynamic analysis practical, through pushing it into new domains and toward semantic bugs, to today's hybrid of graph- and learning-based methods layered on top of program structure.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this slice, all from NDSS 2018, shows program analysis being pointed at whatever platform was newly under threat. ZEUS: Analyzing Safety of Smart Contracts (NDSS 2018) brought abstract-interpretation-style verification to Ethereum contracts precisely because a deployed contract cannot be patched, while K-Miner: Uncovering Memory Corruption in Linux (NDSS 2018) pushed static analysis to a scale most tools could not handle by partitioning the kernel along system-call boundaries. Others adapted classic techniques to new languages and layers: SYNODE (NDSS 2018) tackled injection in Node.js, AceDroid (NDSS 2018) normalized Android access-control checks to find inconsistencies, and Superset Disassembly (NDSS 2018) rebuilt static binary rewriting without brittle heuristics. The common thread was taking well-understood analysis ideas — taint tracking, symbolic reasoning, disassembly — and hardening them for messy, real-world targets.

The next few years were dominated by making symbolic and hybrid execution actually scale, and then by pointing that machinery at microarchitectural bugs. Send Hardest Problems My Way (NDSS 2019) used probabilistic path prioritization to make concolic execution pull its weight inside a fuzzing loop, and Neuro-Symbolic Execution (NDSS 2019) began splicing learned neural constraints into the solver to reach code that pure symbolic execution could not. SymQEMU (NDSS 2021) then made symbolic execution practical on raw binaries through compilation-based instrumentation. In parallel, the Spectre disclosures reshaped the field's agenda: Hunting the Haunter with Haunted RelSE (NDSS 2021) brought relational symbolic execution to speculative leaks, and SpecTaint (NDSS 2021) recast the problem as speculative taint analysis to surface Spectre gadgets. Alongside this, learning entered binary analysis directly through DeepBinDiff (NDSS 2020), which learned program-wide code representations for diffing, while Precisely Characterizing Security Impact via Symbolic Rule Comparison (NDSS 2020) applied symbolic reasoning to the practical problem of triaging security patches.

By the early-to-mid 2020s the targets broadened and the analyses grew more specialized. Context-Sensitive and Directional Concurrency Fuzzing (NDSS 2022) and Cross-Language Attacks (NDSS 2022) confronted concurrency data races and the seams between memory-safe and unsafe languages, while smart-contract analysis matured from ZEUS-style verification toward learning, as in Smarter Contracts (NDSS 2023) with deep transfer learning. Protocol and binary understanding also became a theme of its own, from BinaryInferno (NDSS 2023) inferring binary message formats to Automata-Based detection of protocol state-machine bugs (NDSS 2023). DeGPT (NDSS 2024) was an early sign of the shift ahead, using an LLM to clean up decompiler output, while Faster and Better (NDSS 2024) squeezed more precision out of reaching-definition analysis for IoT firmware.

The most recent NDSS 2026 papers make two trends unmistakable: large language models are now both a tool and a target, and taint-style analysis has spread to ever more exotic software stacks. ProtocolGuard (NDSS 2026) pairs LLM-guided static analysis with dynamic verification to catch protocol non-compliance, and Idioms (NDSS 2026) turbo-charges neural decompilation with well-defined type information, extending the DeGPT trajectory. At the same time, Trust Me, I Know This Function (NDSS 2026) shows the field turning a critical eye on itself by hijacking LLM-based static analysis through bias — a warning that learned analyzers can be fooled. Taint tracking, meanwhile, reaches into modern web and firmware stacks with TranSPArent (NDSS 2026) for single-page-application frameworks and FirmCross (NDSS 2026) for C-Lua hybrid firmware services, while User-Space Dependency-Aware Rehosting (NDSS 2026) keeps dynamic firmware analysis viable. The area today blends decades-old ideas — symbolic execution, taint, reaching definitions — with learned models, even as it starts auditing those models for the same weaknesses it once hunted in code.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this slice of IEEE S&P is squarely in the classical program-analysis tradition: finding specific, dangerous bug classes with careful static and dynamic reasoning. "Precise and Scalable Detection of Double-Fetch Bugs in OS Kernels" (S&P 2018) hunted a subtle kernel race, "Learning from Mutants: Using Code Mutation to Learn and Monitor Invariants of a Cyber-Physical System" (S&P 2018) mined invariants to watch industrial control systems, and "Impossibility of Precise and Sound Termination-Sensitive Security Enforcements" (S&P 2018) staked out the theoretical limits of what enforcement can ever achieve. Even here two threads that would grow were visible: binaries and machine learning. "Asm2Vec" (S&P 2019) learned robust representations of assembly for clone search that survived obfuscation and compiler optimization, while "SoK: Sanitizing for Security" (S&P 2019) took stock of the runtime instrumentation that dynamic bug-finding leans on.

Around 2020 the field visibly diversified along a few fronts. Symbolic and hybrid execution matured for security-specific goals: "SAVIOR: Towards Bug-Driven Hybrid Testing" and "Pangolin: Incremental Hybrid Fuzzing with Polyhedral Path Abstraction" (both S&P 2020) steered concolic execution toward bugs and hard constraints, while "CaSym" (S&P 2019), "Spectector: Principled Detection of Speculative Information Flows" and "Binsec/Rel" (both S&P 2020) turned that machinery on side channels and constant-time code. Binary-level analysis pushed toward practical tooling with "RetroWrite: Statically Instrumenting COTS Binaries for Fuzzing and Sanitization" (S&P 2020), later joined by the disassembly reckoning of "SoK: All You Ever Wanted to Know About x86/x64 Binary Disassembly" (S&P 2021) and structure-recovery work like "OSPREY" (S&P 2021). Simultaneously, smart contracts became a magnet for verification, with "VerX," "VERISMART," and "Semantic Understanding of Smart Contracts" (all S&P 2020) followed by "SmartPulse," "SGUARD" (S&P 2021), and "SAILFISH" (S&P 2022).

Fuzzing kept getting smarter by absorbing analysis rather than replacing it. "BEACON: Directed Grey-Box Fuzzing with Provable Path Pruning," "PATA: Fuzzing with Path Aware Taint Analysis," and "Effective Seed Scheduling for Fuzzing with Graph Centrality Analysis" (all S&P 2022) folded taint tracking, provable pruning, and graph reasoning into the fuzzing loop. Then the ground shifted toward learned models: "Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair with Large Language Models" (S&P 2023) asked whether LLMs could patch real vulnerabilities, and "LLMs Cannot Reliably Identify and Reason About Security Vulnerabilities (Yet?)" (S&P 2024) answered with a hard-nosed benchmark showing they cannot yet be trusted alone, a useful corrective to the hype.

The most recent work reads as a synthesis of these threads. Classical analysis is still advancing on hard targets: "CiRCLE" (S&P 2026) recovers complex data structures in binaries beyond fragmentation, "Contextualizing Sink Knowledge for Java Vulnerability Discovery" and "SFA-Miner" (both S&P 2026) sharpen sink and API-usage reasoning, and "Best of Both Worlds: Effective Foreign Bridge Identification in V8 Embedders" (S&P 2026) attacks native/WebAssembly boundaries. New domains keep appearing, from ZKP circuits in "Language-Agnostic Detection of Computation-Constraint Inconsistencies in ZKP Programs" to deep-learning toolchains in "Your Compiler is Backdooring Your Model" (both S&P 2026). Most tellingly, LLMs are being wired directly into the analysis pipeline rather than judged from outside: "SpecAuditor: Generating Audit Specifications for LLM-Driven Bug Detection," "PortGPT: Towards Automated Backporting Using Large Language Models," and especially "Detecting Privilege Escalation in Polyglot Microservices via Agentic Program Analysis" (all S&P 2026) point to a near future where agentic, LLM-guided program analysis reasons across languages and services, while the sobering 2024 benchmark keeps expectations grounded.

ccs.narrative:
Program analysis for security at CCS has evolved from classical static and dynamic techniques toward ML-augmented analysis pipelines. In 2018, the field produced two contrasting anchors: Securify: Practical Security Analysis of Smart Contracts (CCS 2018) demonstrated sound static verification at blockchain scale, while LEMNA: Explaining Deep Learning based Security Applications (CCS 2018) raised the question of interpretability for neural-network security classifiers. Debin: Predicting Debug Information in Stripped Binaries (CCS 2018) applied ML to binary recovery for the first time at CCS.

The 2019 cohort pushed static analysis to new targets: CryptoGuard: High Precision Detection of Cryptographic Vulnerabilities in Massive-sized Java Projects (CCS 2019) caught API misuse in hundreds of large real-world projects, and Detecting Violations of Differential Privacy (CCS 2018) showed that DP implementations can be automatically tested for correctness. Symbolic-execution-guided fuzzing appeared in Learning to Fuzz from Symbolic Execution with Application to Smart Contracts (CCS 2019).

From 2021, large language model embeddings entered binary analysis. PalmTree: Learning an Assembly Language Model for Instruction Embedding (CCS 2021) pre-trained on assembly to improve clone detection and vulnerability search, followed by SymLM: Predicting Function Names in Stripped Binaries (CCS 2022) and ReSym: Harnessing LLMs to Recover Variable and Data Structure Symbols from Stripped Binaries (CCS 2024), which brought GPT-class models to decompilation symbol recovery.

milestones.title: Securify: Practical Security Analysis of Smart Contracts
milestones.note: Proved or disproved smart contract security properties via compliance patterns, becoming the field's reference analyzer.

milestones.note: Pre-trained a BERT-style model on assembly, providing universal instruction embeddings for downstream binary analysis tasks.

milestones.note: Predicted stripped binary function names using execution-aware context embeddings, advancing automatic decompilation.

milestones.note: Applied large language models to recover rich symbol information from stripped binaries during decompilation.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this slice splits along two lines that would define the decade. One is the explosion of smart-contract analysis: "Securify: Practical Security Analysis of Smart Contracts" (CCS 2018) and "ZEUS: Analyzing Safety of Smart Contracts" (NDSS 2018) brought static and symbolic reasoning to Ethereum bytecode, while "teEther: Gnawing at Ethereum to Automatically Exploit Smart Contracts" (USENIX 2018) pushed past detection into automatic exploit generation. The other line is a rethinking of test generation, headlined by "QSYM: A Practical Concolic Execution Engine Tailored for Hybrid Fuzzing" (USENIX 2018), which showed that pairing a fast, loosely-coupled concolic engine with a fuzzer could beat either alone. Alongside these, classic taint tracking kept maturing on real systems, as in "Sensitive Information Tracking in Commodity IoT" (USENIX 2018).

The 2019-2020 stretch is where the field both deepened its foundations and started leaning on machine learning. Hybrid fuzzing got sharper with "Send Hardest Problems My Way: Probabilistic Path Prioritization for Hybrid Fuzzing" (NDSS 2019), "GREYONE: Data Flow Sensitive Fuzzing" (USENIX 2020), and the bug-targeted "SAVIOR: Towards Bug-Driven Hybrid Testing" (S&P 2020), while "RetroWrite: Statically Instrumenting COTS Binaries for Fuzzing and Sanitization" (S&P 2020) made these techniques work on binaries without source. The community also took stock of its own tools, notably "SoK: Sanitizing for Security" (S&P 2019). Meanwhile learned representations arrived in force for binary analysis, from "Asm2Vec" (S&P 2019) to "DeepBinDiff" (NDSS 2020) and later "PalmTree: Learning an Assembly Language Model for Instruction Embedding" (CCS 2021). Smart-contract work matured from bug-finding toward provable guarantees with "VerX: Safety Verification of Smart Contracts" (S&P 2020) and "eThor: Practical and Provably Sound Static Analysis of Ethereum Smart Contracts" (CCS 2020), and analysis stretched to new threat models in "Spectector: Principled Detection of Speculative Information Flows" (S&P 2020).

The most recent shift is the arrival of large language models as both a tool and a subject of scrutiny. "Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair with Large Language Models" (S&P 2023) asked whether off-the-shelf models could fix security bugs, and "LLMs Cannot Reliably Identify and Reason About Security Vulnerabilities (Yet?)" (S&P 2024) answered the mirror-image question with a sober benchmark showing their limits. By 2026 the frontier is hybrid: "ProtocolGuard: Detecting Protocol Non-compliance Bugs via LLM-guided Static Analysis and Dynamic Verification" (NDSS 2026) folds LLM guidance into a classic static-plus-dynamic pipeline, "Idioms: A Simple and Effective Framework for Turbo-Charging Local Neural Decompilation with Well-Defined Types" (NDSS 2026) applies learning to decompilation, and "Trust Me, I Know This Function: Hijacking LLM Static Analysis using Bias" (NDSS 2026) shows the new attack surface these models open up. At the same time the durable techniques keep advancing on hard targets, with taint-style analysis reaching hybrid firmware in "FirmCross: Detecting Taint-style Vulnerabilities in Modern C-Lua Hybrid Web Services" and modern web apps in "TranSPArent: Taint-style Vulnerability Detection in Generic Single Page Applications" (both NDSS 2026). The trajectory is clear: from hand-built static and symbolic analyzers, through learned representations, to a present where LLMs are woven into analysis pipelines even as researchers measure and probe their weaknesses.
